questions.subject: DATA_STRUCTURES
questions.stem: Analyze the scenario presented. Using the adjacency lists 0:[1,2], 1:[0,2,3], 2:[0,1,4], 3:[1,4,5], 4:[2,3,5], 5:[3,4] with neighbors visited in increasing order, which sequence is the breadth-first traversal from vertex 1?

options.misconception: reverses the discovery order
uses depth-first search instead
rotates the start vertex to the end

questions.explanation: BFS uses a queue and discovers all neighbors of a vertex before going deeper. Starting at 1, the visit order is 1 -> 0 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4 -> 5; the other option is the opposite traversal strategy.
questions.hint: Use a queue and enqueue neighbors in increasing order.

questions.subject: DATA_STRUCTURES
questions.stem: Find the answer using the stated rules. In the unweighted connected graph 0:[1,2], 1:[0,2,3], 2:[0,1,4], 3:[1,4,5], 4:[2,3,5], 5:[3,4], how many edges are on a shortest path from vertex 1 to vertex 0?

options.misconception: counts vertices on the path instead of edges
assumes an unreachable target when the graph is connected
off by one in the level count

questions.explanation: In an unweighted graph a BFS from 1 discovers 0 at level 1, which is the number of edges on the shortest path. A path with 1 edges has 2 vertices, which is why counting vertices is the frequent slip.
questions.hint: Run BFS from the source and read off the level at which the target is discovered.

questions.subject: DATA_STRUCTURES
questions.stem: Think about the following task. Using Kruskal's algorithm on the weighted edges [0-1:4, 0-2:2, 1-2:1, 1-3:5, 2-3:8, 2-4:10, 3-4:2, 3-5:6, 4-5:3], what is the total weight of a minimum spanning tree?

options.misconception: takes the five cheapest edges without skipping cycles
adds every edge weight instead of selecting the spanning tree
adds one extra edge weight

questions.explanation: Sorting edges by weight and accepting an edge only when it joins two different components gives a spanning tree of total weight 13. Adding every edge, or the five cheapest without cycle checks, overshoots because it keeps redundant edges.
questions.hint: Process edges cheapest first and skip any edge whose endpoints are already connected.

questions.subject: DATA_STRUCTURES
questions.stem: A typical exam item asks this: After one pass of selection sort on the array 7, 5, 1, 9, 2, 6, 8, what is the array state?

options.misconception: applies the wrong rearrangement for this pass
leaves the array unchanged as if no pass occurred
assumes a single pass fully sorts the whole array

questions.explanation: One pass of selection sort moves only the element being placed in that pass; the prefix it touches becomes ordered but the rest stays as before, yielding 1, 5, 7, 9, 2, 6, 8. Thinking the whole array is sorted after one pass is a common misconception.
questions.hint: Simulate exactly one outer-loop iteration, not the entire sort.

questions.subject: DATA_STRUCTURES
questions.stem: This problem calls for a trace. Counting sort is applied to the digit array 2, 4, 0, 2, 5, 5 with values in 0..5. What is the sorted output?

options.misconception: expands the counts in descending order instead of ascending
reports the unsorted input rather than the counting-sort result
rotates the sorted output by one position

questions.explanation: counting sort tallies each digit then expands the counts in ascending order. Counting sort runs in O(n+k) time, and reading a count slot is different from reading the sorted output array.
questions.hint: Tally occurrences of each digit in 0..5 first, then read the requested quantity.

questions.subject: DATA_STRUCTURES
questions.stem: Work from the stated assumptions. Which sort uses O(1) auxiliary space and is in-place with O(n log n) average time?

options.misconception: counting sort is not comparison-based and uses O(k) space
insertion sort is O(n^2) on average
merge sort needs O(n) auxiliary space for merging

questions.explanation: Quick sort fits all the stated constraints; each alternative fails one of them, whether stability, worst-case time, or auxiliary space. Matching every clause of the question to a known property avoids picking a sort that satisfies only part of it.
questions.hint: Check stability, worst-case time, and space separately for each candidate.

questions.subject: DATA_STRUCTURES
questions.stem: Use the facts presented to decide. Using the recurrence F(0)=0, F(1)=1, F(k)=F(k-1)+F(k-2), what is F(13)?

options.misconception: advances the recurrence by one index too far
adds an extra term as if two base cases overlapped
returns the previous Fibonacci number by stopping one step early

questions.explanation: Building the table from the base cases up, F(13) = 233. Each earlier value is reused rather than recomputed, which is what makes the dynamic-programming version linear; off-by-one index errors produce the neighboring Fibonacci values in the options.
questions.hint: Build the sequence from F(0) upward, adding the two previous terms each step.

questions.subject: DATA_STRUCTURES
questions.stem: Consider this particular instance. Given house values [4, 9, 1, 1, 10, 2, 9], what is the maximum sum obtainable by choosing non-adjacent houses?

options.misconception: takes only the single largest value
adds every house and ignores the adjacency constraint
subtracts a value as if one house had to be removed

questions.explanation: At each house the optimal value is the max of taking it plus the best up to two houses back, versus skipping it; evaluating that recurrence gives 28. Summing all values violates the no-adjacent rule.
questions.hint: Keep two running bests: best ending at the previous house and best ending two houses back.

questions.subject: DATA_STRUCTURES
questions.stem: Apply the concept to this instance. What is the length of the longest common subsequence of "dccadd" and "bdacbbc"?

options.misconception: assumes a common subsequence can be as long as the shorter string
stops one cell early in the table
adds one from an inclusive diagonal index

questions.explanation: Filling the LCS table uses dp[i][j] = dp[i-1][j-1]+1 when characters match, otherwise the max of the cell above and the cell to the left; the final cell is 3. A common substring would be stricter, but a subsequence may skip characters.
questions.hint: Build an (m+1) by (n+1) table and read the bottom-right cell.

questions.subject: DATA_STRUCTURES
questions.stem: A problem for careful thought: When F(n) with F(0)=0, F(1)=1 is computed by recursive memoization, how many distinct subproblem values F(k) are ever computed, for k from 0 up to n = 11?

options.misconception: forgets one of the two base-case states
counts repeated calls of naive recursion rather than distinct cached states
omits both base cases from the state count

questions.explanation: Memoization computes each state F(0) through F(n) exactly once and reuses it, so there are 12 distinct values. Naive recursion makes exponentially many calls but the cache collapses them to one per state.
questions.hint: List the indices k for which F(k) is stored; do not count repeated lookups.

questions.subject: DATA_STRUCTURES
questions.stem: Compute the result for this case. Using the greedy coin change algorithm with denominations 1, 5, 10, 25 (taking the largest possible coin first), how many coins make change for 62 cents?

options.misconception: counts denominations that divide the amount rather than coins used
adds one coin from rounding up a remainder
uses one coin of value one for every unit of the amount

questions.explanation: Taking the largest coin greedily gives 2 quarter(s) then dimes, nickels and pennies, totaling 5 coins. Counting denominations that divide the amount or using only pennies ignores how many coins are actually selected.
questions.hint: Repeatedly subtract the largest coin not exceeding the remaining amount.

questions.learningObjective: demonstrate understanding of divide and conquer
questions.stem: This item tests your reasoning. Merge sort is applied to an array of 64 elements. How many merge operations are performed in total?

options.misconception: doubles the count as if every element merged separately
counts only the top level of splitting
counts one too many merges or drops the base level

questions.explanation: A merge combines two sorted runs into one, reducing the number of runs by one; going from 64 singleton runs to one run takes 63 merges.
questions.hint: Each merge reduces the run count by one, from n runs down to one.

questions.subject: DATA_STRUCTURES
questions.stem: Apply the concept to this instance. Which property must hold for a greedy algorithm to be provably optimal?

options.misconception: input size monotonicity is not a standard correctness condition
optimal substructure is necessary but not sufficient for greedy choice
a large search space does not justify greedy correctness

questions.explanation: The greedy-choice property is the needed condition; the alternatives either describe a different technique or state a property that is insufficient on its own. Greedy proofs typically show that an optimal solution can be transformed to include the greedy choice.
questions.hint: Think of the exchange argument that converts an optimal solution into the greedy one.

questions.subject: DATA_STRUCTURES
questions.stem: In this setting, what follows? Which technique suits the 0/1 knapsack problem, where items cannot be split?

options.misconception: plain divide and conquer recomputes the same subproblems
greedy fails for 0/1 knapsack because items are indivisible
without a table the overlapping subproblems are not reused

questions.explanation: Dynamic programming is the appropriate method because of how the problem's constraints interact with the technique's assumptions; applying the others either wastes work or gives a suboptimal result. Whether items are divisible is the decisive difference between the two knapsack forms.
questions.hint: Ask whether the problem has the greedy-choice property or needs tabulated subproblems.

questions.subject: DATA_STRUCTURES
questions.stem: Reason carefully about this case. Inserting the words door, cart, batman, car, bar into an empty trie (one node per distinct prefix plus a root), how many nodes does the trie contain?

options.misconception: counts every character of every word separately instead of sharing prefixes
counts only the root and one terminal node per word
forgets the root node of the trie

questions.explanation: Each distinct prefix gets its own node and words sharing a prefix share those nodes; with a root the total is 16. Counting all characters of all words double-counts shared prefixes such as the common opening letters here.
questions.hint: List every distinct prefix of every word, then add one for the root.

questions.subject: DATA_STRUCTURES
questions.stem: Analyze the given configuration. Union-find over elements 0..7 starts with each element its own component. After unions (3,2), (4,5), (6,3), how many components remain?

options.misconception: adds one from miscounting the initial number of components
assumes every union failed and all elements remain separate
subtracts one per union without checking whether endpoints were already connected

questions.explanation: Each union merges two components only when its endpoints were in different sets; starting from 8 singletons the given unions leave 5 components. Subtracting blindly for every union overcounts merges when endpoints were already connected.
questions.hint: Track the representative of each element and only merge when two representatives differ.

questions.subject: DATA_STRUCTURES
questions.stem: A learner encounters this problem. A Bloom filter has m = 11 bits and hash functions h1(x)=x mod m, h2(x)=(2x+1) mod m. Which bit positions are set when key 32 is inserted?

options.misconception: swaps the two hash formulas
adds two to each hashed position
uses k+1 style hashes instead of the defined h1 and h2

questions.explanation: Computing h1(32) and h2(32) gives bit positions 10, 10. Both functions must be applied; using only one or shifting the formulas sets the wrong bits and can create false negatives if checked inconsistently.
questions.hint: Evaluate h1 and h2 separately with the same modulus m, then list both positions.

questions.subject: DATA_STRUCTURES
questions.learningObjective: demonstrate understanding of skip lists / others
questions.stem: Determine the value in question. What is the expected time to search for an element in a skip list of n items with geometric promotion?

options.misconception: assumes direct addressing without any traversal
treats the express lanes as if they did not skip nodes
multiplies a linear scan by the number of levels

questions.explanation: O(log n) follows from the geometric distribution of tower heights: with promotion probability 1/2 the expected tower height is 2, and the express lanes give logarithmic expected search time. Assuming no promotion or a linear scan ignores the skipping structure.
questions.hint: Think of the geometric series for tower heights and how express lanes shorten the path.

questions.subject: DATA_STRUCTURES
questions.stem: In a quiz setting, answer this. For a sorted array of n = 15 elements, how many key comparisons does binary search make in the worst case?

options.misconception: off by one below the tree depth by forgetting the root comparison
doubles the depth instead of recognizing that each step halves the interval
off by one above the depth by counting the empty final interval

questions.explanation: A binary search over n = 2^4 - 1 elements builds a complete decision tree of height 3, so the deepest leaf needs 4 comparisons; each comparison halves the remaining range, which is why the count is logarithmic and not linear.
questions.hint: Write n + 1 as a power of two; the number of comparisons is that exponent.

questions.subject: DATA_STRUCTURES
questions.stem: Review the case and choose wisely. For the recurrence T(n) = 4T(n/2) + n, what is the tight asymptotic bound of T(n)?

options.misconception: applies the case-2 log factor even when f(n) is not Θ(n^{log_b a})
takes only the largest f(n) power seen in the recurrence table
takes only the trivial bound and ignores both recursive work and f(n)

questions.explanation: Here log base 2 of 4 equals 2, so the recursive work is Θ(n^2); comparing that exponent with the 1 in f(n) selects the Master Theorem case that yields Θ(n^2).
questions.hint: Compute log_b(a) and compare it with the exponent of f(n).

questions.subject: DATA_STRUCTURES
questions.stem: Determine the outcome of this case. A dynamic array starts with capacity 2 and doubles its capacity whenever it is full. After 10 append operations, how many element copies have occurred in total?

options.misconception: assumes exactly one resize of the initial capacity occurs
counts only the m insertions and ignores every resize copy
overestimates by imagining a copy on every append

questions.explanation: Resizes happen when size reaches capacity; the copied amounts are 2, 4, and so on up to the last resize, summing to 14. Because each element is copied at most once per doubling level, the total is below 2m, giving amortized O(1) per append.
questions.hint: Track size and capacity together; a resize copies the current size, then capacity doubles.

questions.subject: DATA_STRUCTURES
questions.stem: Determine the correct result here. For an input of size n = 7071, what is the worst-case auxiliary space (excluding the input) used by recursive binary search?

options.misconception: counts one stack frame or buffer slot per input element
mixes the time bound of a sort into its space bound
assumes no call stack or auxiliary buffer is ever allocated

questions.explanation: Auxiliary space counts extra memory beyond the input. For recursive binary search the dominant extra allocation grows as O(log n); call-stack frames or a temporary buffer scale with that quantity, and this measure is distinct from the algorithm's running time.
questions.hint: Separate time from space: ask how deep the recursion goes or how large the extra buffer is.
